--- title: "Quarto II & Objects/Vectors/Lists" subtitle: "Lecture 4" date: "August 27, 2026" format: revealjs: theme: [dark, slides.scss] filters: - webr editor: markdown: wrap: 72 --- ## Checklist {.smaller} -- Did you engage with the prepare material? -- The attendance sheet will be passed around! Please sign-in. -- Quiz released Tuesday (due Friday) on Moodle ``` --- lowest quiz-score dropped --- no late policy on quizzes ``` -- Do you know how to get help in ST115? -- Open up RStudio and have a .qmd file ready to go! -- I have uploaded a `CommonErrors.qmd` file to Moodle. Go ahead and download + open this as well! We will talk about common errors today. ## Warm-up{.smaller} What is the difference between 
```{r}
# this
```
```{r}
#| echo: false
```
## Warm-up{.smaller} What do these do? -- echo: -- eval: -- message: -- warning: Hint: Create a r code chunk with the following, and try it for yourself! ``` 2+2 warning("Something might be wrong!") message("Here's some information for you.") ``` ## Note Spacing is important here! (and it reads nicer) #| eval: false # Questions # YAML ## YAML {.smaller} We have mappings and keys! You can think of the "map" as a YAML option. You can think of the "key" as the value the option takes on. ``` --- title: "My Document" --- ``` title is the "map" and "My Document" is the key! Note: When we are working with a simple string, the quotes are optional. When you are working with things likes numbers that you want to be treated as text, quotes are necessary. [Options](https://quarto-tdg.org/yaml.html) ## YAML {.smaller} What's the difference? ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **Example 1** ```{=html} 
---
title: "Test Document"
author:
name: Elijah Meyer
affiliation: NC State University
---
``` **Example 2** ```{=html} 
---
title: "Test Document"
author:
- name: Elijah Meyer
affiliation: NC State University
---
``` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Example 3** ```{=html} 
---
title: "Test Document"
author:
  - name: Elijah Meyer
    affiliation: NC State University
---
``` ::: ::: ## YAML The `-` is necessary when we have a list item (an item that we could have multiple of) ``` author └── list item ├── name └── affiliation ``` **Most** (not all) YAML headings require indentation. This is a good habit to get into early. # Questions ## Common Errors Download the **CommonErrors.qmd** from Moodle, and open it up on your computer! Try and fix the code so it renders a document. # Don't cheat ## Common Errors -- Code chunks not closed -- Incorrect code preventing rendering -- YAML # Questions ## Challenge Question (if time) {.smaller} -- Make a new quarto document -- Title is "Iris-Practice" and put yourself as the author -- Pull up the help file for the `iris` data set (and discuss if we should include the help file in the Quarto document or not) -- Make a level-2 section header and title it "Description" -- Copy the description text into your Quarto file -- Answer the question: What is larger, the mean or median Petal Width? # Questions # Objects, Vectors, and Lists ## R Objects When we create something in R, such as a number, a word, or a collection of values, R stores it as an object. ``` x <- 10 x + 5 ``` ## Vectors A vector is a collection of values. `c` stands for combine (you can think about this as collection if you would like!) ``` scores <- c(85, 92, 78, 90, 88) ``` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` num [1:5] 85 92 78 90 88 ``` ::: ::: What type of vector is this? A numeric vector or a character vector? ## Vectors We will talk about character vs numeric now, and talk about more types of data types + data coercion later in the semester! ``` cities <- c("Raleigh", "Durham", "Chapel Hill") ``` We can think about characters as **Text** data. These data will have " " around them. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` chr [1:3] "Raleigh" "Durham" "Chapel Hill" ``` ::: ::: ## Indexing{.smaller} Sometimes, we want to only look at a subset of our vector. On your own, please run the following code, and take note of what we discover. ``` data <- c(4,6,7,3,2,5,8) a) data[2] b) data[3:6] c) data[c(1,4,6)] d) data[-5] e) data[-c(2,3,5,7)] ``` # Questions ## Lists{.smaller} A list is an object that can contain different kinds of objects! So far, we have discussed character vectors and numeric vectors. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} student.temp <- c("Alice", 19, 92, 88, 95) student <- list( name = "Alice", age = 19, scores = c(92, 88, 95) ) ``` ::: ## Lists{.smaller} Let's play around with this list using the `$`. Run the following code and see what we learn. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} student$name student$gpa student$scores mean(student$scores) ``` ::: ## Lists{.smaller} So why are lists useful? Let's compare our `student` list vs say the data frame `iris` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species 1 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2 setosa 2 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2 setosa 3 4.7 3.2 1.3 0.2 setosa 4 4.6 3.1 1.5 0.2 setosa 5 5.0 3.6 1.4 0.2 setosa 6 5.4 3.9 1.7 0.4 setosa ``` ::: ::: What's the same? What's different? ## Lists vs Data Frames ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` name age major score 1 Alice 19 Biology 92 2 Alice 19 Biology 88 3 Alice 19 Biology 95 ``` ::: ::: ## Summary The components (variables) of a data frame have to be the same length! Lists, they do not. A data frame is designed for: Many observations of the same set of variables. A list is designed for: Putting different kinds of information together. Or: A list organizes objects; a data frame organizes observations into rows and variables into columns. # Questions? ## Challenge Question (if time){.smaller} Compare the mean Petal Length of each of the three species of flowers Hint: The iris dataset is broken down in groups rows of 50 (sequential) for each flower. Next, create a list for one specific flower that has the following names, and include the appropriate values. -- species -- petal_information (mean value, median value) -- sepal_information (mean value, median value)

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
